title: VeriSimpl: Robust Optimization Modeling from Natural Language using Simplification-based Verification
one_liner: Turn a word problem into an optimization model and then verify it by asking the model to reason about simpler derived cases generated by the solver.
lead: A language model can often write a solver program that runs without syntax errors. That does not mean the program matches the intended optimization problem. A missed constraint, a reversed inequality, or an unnecessary decision variable can produce a cleanly executing but wrong model. VeriSimpl addresses that gap by making verification easier than full direct checking. It asks the solver to simplify the candidate formulation into smaller diagnostic cases, then asks the language model whether those simpler cases still agree with the original task description. The simplification matters because local reasoning about a reduced subproblem is easier than reasoning about the full model all at once.

problem.h2: Why natural-language-to-optimization systems make subtle mistakes
paras: An optimization model has to translate plain-language requirements into exact variables, objective terms, and constraints. A solver will happily optimize the wrong thing if the model is internally consistent. So execution success is a weak test: it only shows the syntax is valid and the solver found a feasible or optimal solution under the written rules.

Directly asking a language model whether the entire formulation is correct is also unreliable. The full model may contain many interacting constraints, and the language description may combine several conditions in one paragraph. Global checking overloads the reasoning step, so the model can miss a local mismatch even when that mismatch is easy to see once isolated because several interacting rules compete for one limited reasoning pass.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Use the solver to generate simpler diagnostic versions of the candidate formulation, then verify those cases against the natural-language description so errors become locally visible.

panels.title: 1. Start from a word problem
panels.viz_args: The user describes costs, capacities, and requirements in plain language.
panels.caption: The system must translate those statements into a formal optimization model.

panels.title: 2. Candidate model may run but still be wrong
panels.caption: A solver result is not proof of semantic correctness.

panels.title: 3. Simplify the formulation
panels.viz_args: Fix some variables or remove selected constraints to create easier diagnostic cases.
panels.caption: The simplified case preserves one local question while reducing the reasoning load.

panels.title: 4. Ask the language model to verify the simpler case
panels.caption: Local checks expose whether one constraint block or variable role is mis-specified.

panels.title: 5. Repair the original formulation
panels.caption: The system uses high-precision diagnostic failures to revise the candidate model.

steps.text: The language model maps the text description into variables, constraints, and an objective for a solver.
The solver fixes some variables, drops or isolates some constraints, or narrows the feasible set so the resulting subproblem tests one local aspect of the formulation.
Each simplified subproblem is converted into a targeted verification prompt that asks whether the reduced case still matches the user's intent.
Agreement between the simplified model and the task description raises confidence; disagreement points to a concrete place where the formulation is wrong.
Use the diagnostic findings to edit the full model and rerun the cycle until the verification checks stop failing.

paras: The paper changes verification from a single global judgment into a sequence of local checks. The main idea is that the solver is not only an execution engine. It is also a tool for constructing simpler counterfactual cases that make semantic errors easier to detect.

hidden.name: whether each local part of the formulation matches the intended rule
paras: The important quantity is semantic alignment at the level of individual modeling choices. A full formulation may fail because one capacity constraint is reversed, one index range is wrong, or one variable should have been binary rather than continuous. Those are local faults, but their effect can be hidden inside a large valid program.

VeriSimpl exposes those local faults by simplifying the formulation until a diagnostic case depends mainly on one suspect choice. If the simplified case no longer matches the natural-language description, the system learns not just that the model is wrong but why it is wrong.

heat.caption: Dark cells mark the local formulation choices that matter for semantic correctness and become visible after simplification.

reads.html: The goal is to verify each important rule in isolation instead of trusting one pass over the whole model.

Simplification-based verification converts a hard global equivalence question into easier local entailment checks, because the reduced subproblem holds the global context fixed while varying one modeling dimension.

paras: The solver already understands the formal structure of the candidate model. It can therefore create reduced instances that preserve some constraints while freezing others. That turns a dense formulation into a smaller case whose intended answer is easier to reason about from the text description.

The language model is stronger at this smaller task because fewer interacting parts compete for focus during one reasoning pass. If a reduced case asks only whether one capacity rule is enforced or whether one decision variable should be active, the reasoning burden drops. A wrong answer in that case points directly to the offending rule block.

The verification signal is high precision because a failed local check usually maps to a specific repair. The full loop improves modeling accuracy by alternating between solver-based simplification and language-based semantic judgment, so each component contributes what it is good at.

stages.s: Language model writes a candidate solver formulation
Solver simplifies the formulation into diagnostic subproblems
Language model checks each subproblem against the original intent
A formulation whose local parts have been individually checked for semantic correctness

math.words: One diagnostic step fixes part of the decision vector and checks whether the reduced feasible set still agrees with the text description.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the original task includes shipping goods from warehouses to stores under capacity limits.
Fix the shipping decisions for all but one warehouse and ask whether the remaining reduced problem still reflects the stated capacity rule for that warehouse.
If the simplified case permits more shipments than the text allows, the error is local and visible.
That local contradiction tells the system which constraint block needs repair.

math.note: The paper uses several simplification dimensions, but they all serve the same purpose: isolate one semantic question while keeping the rest of the model fixed.

charts.title: Direct generation without local verification
charts.note: A model can produce code that runs while still missing the intended optimization logic.

charts.title: VeriSimpl
charts.note: The gain comes from using simplified diagnostic cases to expose which local rule is wrong, so revisions are informed rather than blind because each failed check points to a specific repair target.

items.b: The simplification may hide the original error.
items.html: If the reduced case removes the interaction that causes the bug, the diagnostic query may approve a formulation that still fails in the full problem.

items.b: Verification prompts can still be misread.
items.html: A language model may misunderstand a diagnostic question, especially when the natural-language task description is itself ambiguous.

items.b: Too many diagnostic queries can raise cost.
items.html: If every candidate formulation triggers many solver calls and many language-model checks, the approach may become expensive for large modeling tasks.
Choose simplifications that isolate likely error sources, keep the diagnostic prompts tightly tied to the original wording, and stop once the remaining checks no longer reveal distinct local faults.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Take a small benchmark of transportation, scheduling, and knapsack-style word problems. For each problem, generate a solver formulation with a language model and compare two workflows: direct generation alone and VeriSimpl with simplification-based verification.

Track not only whether the solver runs, but whether the final formulation matches a reference model and how often the verification stage points to the correct faulty rule. The demo should show that local diagnostic cases improve final correctness because they turn vague failure into a concrete repair target.
demo.metric_eq: formulation_accuracy = correct_models / total_models ; diagnostic_precision = correct_fault_flags / total_fault_flags
demo.closing: The main evidence is a higher rate of semantically correct formulations, supported by diagnostic signals that identify which part of the model needed revision.
